Generative AI…

title: Appendix D. Impact of Within- and Across-Cluster Citation and Early Adoption on Citeability within and beyond Corpus
text:
Two questions on what predicts how often a corpus paper is cited.
Early adoption: does entering a technology cluster early pay off?
Citation breadth: does citing within one’s own cluster or across clusters pay off?
Each estimated overall, across all 16 technology clusters, and separately per cluster.
Descriptive and observational; no causal identification.

title: Appendix D. Impact of Within- and Across-Cluster Citation and Early Adoption on Citeability within and beyond Corpus
text:
Shared Setup

Method

Sample: corpus papers present in the within-corpus citation network, each with a technology cluster and a publication year.
Two outcomes, reported side by side:

Within Corpus — local citations, citations received from other corpus articles.
Total — global citations, citations received from anywhere.

Model family: negative-binomial GAM (mgcv::gam, family = nb()), appropriate for over-dispersed counts.
Publication age (age = 2026 − PY) entered as a smooth, so no decay shape is assumed.
Age is discrete; the basis dimension is capped below the number of distinct ages available.
Overall models additionally control for cluster citeability, the mean global citations of the paper’s cluster.
Per-cluster models omit that control, since it is constant within a cluster.
Coefficients are on the log scale of the expected citation count.
Code: 30_academic_foundation/07_citation_network.R.

title: Appendix D. Impact of Within- and Across-Cluster Citation and Early Adoption on Citeability within and beyond Corpus
text:
Early Adoption

Method

Predictor: early adoption score = publication year − year of the earliest paper in the same technology cluster.
Lower score = earlier entry into the cluster; 0 = the cluster’s first paper.
Negative coefficient = earlier papers accumulate more citations.
Overall specification: citations ~ early adoption score + cluster citeability + s(age).
Per-cluster specification: citations ~ early adoption score, fitted separately for each of the 16 clusters.
Output: impact_early_adoption_per_cluster.csv / .md.

Rows are the 16 technology clusters; cells give the coefficient with its p-value in parentheses.
Sign indicates direction: negative = earlier papers more cited, positive = later papers more cited.

title: Appendix D. Impact of Within- and Across-Cluster Citation and Early Adoption on Citeability within and beyond Corpus
section: Citing Within and Across Technology Clusters
text:
Citing Within and Across Technology Clusters

Method

Two predictors, both counted on citations the paper makes, not receives:

wi — citations to papers of its own technology cluster.
ac — citations to papers of other technology clusters.

Both standardised by opportunity, since early papers have fewer papers available to cite:

wi divided by the papers published in the same cluster before that year.
ac divided by the papers published in all other clusters before that year.

Papers with an undefined standardised score, that is no prior papers to cite, are dropped.
Overall specification: citations ~ wi + ac + cluster citeability + s(age).
Per-cluster specification: citations ~ wi + ac + s(age), fitted separately for each of the 16 clusters.
Output: impact_citations_per_cluster.csv / .md.



Results

Overall, across all 16 technology clusters:

title: Appendix B. Supplementary Analyses to Analysis 1
text:
Temporal Trajectories

Method

Sample: empirical consumer-technology articles, 2000–2026, assigned to one of the 16 technology clusters.
Unit: mention. An article naming several technologies contributes one mention per technology.
One model per cluster. Negative-binomial GAM of yearly mentions on a smooth of publication year.
Offset: all technology mentions of that year, so each cluster is modelled as a share of technology research rather than as a raw count.
Numerator and denominator are affected alike by the partial year 2026, which therefore stays in.
Basis dimension capped at k = 5.
Peak = maximum of the fitted curve, reported in Table 1.
Code: 10_semantic_mapping/10_temporal_gam.R.



Results

Figure 1 shows one panel per cluster.
Line = fitted share from the model. Points = observed annual share.
Vertical scales differ between panels, so the shape of a trajectory is comparable across clusters but its level is not.
A curve rising or falling across the whole period peaks at a boundary year in Table 1.
A curve cresting inside the period peaks at that year.




Table 1: Total mentions, peak year and peak share of each technology cluster within consumer-technology research, estimated with a negative-binomial generalized additive model of yearly mentions on a smooth of publication year, offset by all technology mentions of that year. Mentions are the cluster’s total mentions across 2000-2026, counted once per article and technology. The peak is the maximum of the fitted curve; a peak in the first or last year of the observation period indicates a cluster that declines or rises throughout rather than one that crests within it. The \(p\)-value tests the smooth against a flat trend. The fitted curves for all clusters are shown in Appendix B.

title: Appendix B. Supplementary Analyses to Analysis 1
text:
Journal Technology Mix

Method

Seven marketing journals: IJRM, JAMS, JCP, JCR, JM, JMR, MkSc.
Sample: empirical consumer-technology articles, 2000–2026, with a technology cluster assigned.
Unit: mention; an article naming several technologies contributes one mention per technology.
Counts cross-tabulated as journals (7) × technology clusters (16).


Deviation Test

Question: does a journal’s technology mix differ from the corpus as a whole?
Baseline b: overall technology cluster shares across the whole corpus, b_k = (Σ_j n_jk) / N.
Baseline includes the journal being tested, so all seven rows are read against one fixed reference point rather than seven shifting ones.
Validity: each mention falls in exactly one technology cluster, so a journal’s shares sum to 1 and the composition is proper; Dirichlet-multinomial applies.
Prior: Dirichlet, concentration α_k = K · b_k with K = 16 technology clusters, identical for every journal.
Prior mean = baseline, i.e. “this journal’s mix matches the corpus”.
Prior mass Σα_k = K, the same total weight as a flat Dirichlet(1, …, 1), redistributed proportionally rather than uniformly; equivalent to 16 pseudo-mentions of evidence for the null.
Effect: shrinks each journal toward the baseline, so small journals are pulled almost fully to the null and marks are harder to earn.
Posterior: Dirichlet-multinomial conjugacy, Dirichlet(α_k + n_jk) for journal j.
Sampling: gamma normalization, g_k ~ Gamma(α_k + n_jk, 1) then p_k = g_k / Σ g_k; 20,000 draws per journal, each a 16-vector summing to 1; single fixed seed.
Deviation per draw: d_k = p_k − b_k.
Interval: equal-tailed 95% credible interval, 2.5th and 97.5th percentile of the draws, read off the empirical quantiles.
Intervals marginal per cell, no multiplicity correction across the 7 × 16 cells.
Marks: ^1^ interval entirely above zero, ^2^ entirely below, blank spans zero.
Blank conflates no effect with too little data.
Marks concern share of a journal’s output, not counts; a small journal can be marked on modest absolute numbers.
Corpus is a census, so intervals generalize to the ongoing publishing process rather than to an unknown fixed quantity.




Results

Table 2 reports mentions per technology cluster and journal.
Rows are the 16 technology clusters, alphabetical with Other last; Total gives the cluster size across all seven journals.
Cell shares are row-wise, the share of the cluster’s mentions falling in that journal.
Marks are column-wise, on the journal’s own technology composition, so cell share and mark use different denominators.
^1^ a cluster credibly over-represented in that journal relative to its corpus-wide share, ^2^ credibly under-represented, blank no credible deviation.





Table 2: Distribution of consumer-technology mentions across the seven journals. Total gives the mentions of the technology cluster across all journals and its share of all mentions; the journal columns give the mentions of that cluster in the journal and its share of the cluster total. The marks are computed column-wise, on the journal’s own technology composition: 1 marks a technology cluster whose 95% credible interval lies entirely above its corpus-wide share, 2 one that lies entirely below it.

title: Appendix E. Supplementary Analyses to Analysis 3
text:
To fit the technology-clustering model reported in the main text, we swept the embedding model, the deduplication threshold, the number of clusters (\(k\)), and the number of UMAP dimensions used for clustering, evaluating each combination on silhouette, Davies-Bouldin, and Calinski-Harabasz scores, and, for the dimensionality sweep, trustworthiness against the original embedding space.


We compared three sentence-embedding models — sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2, BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5, and nomic-ai/nomic-embed-text-v1.5 — across every tested combination of \(k\) and deduplication threshold (Table 1). all-MiniLM-L6-v2 achieved the highest mean silhouette score overall (0.435), ahead of BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 (0.415) and nomic-ai/nomic-embed-text-v1.5 (0.408), and was therefore selected as the embedding model for the final clustering solution.

Holding the embedding model and deduplication threshold fixed, silhouette scores rose gradually across the swept range of \(k = 10\) to \(k = 20\), without a clear inflection point marking a single statistical optimum (Table 2): \(k = 16\) reached a silhouette of 0.436, the next value tested (\(k = 17\)) offered no improvement (0.433), and the score climbed gradually through the top of the swept range (\(k = 20\): 0.471). Because the statistical criteria did not identify a single unambiguous optimum, we prioritized interpretability: \(k = 16\) produced clusters that mapped onto substantively distinct, non-overlapping technology domains upon manual inspection, and we report it as the final solution while acknowledging that larger solutions were better by silhouette alone.

Temporal Trajectories

Method

Sample: empirical consumer-technology articles, 2000–2026, assigned to one of the 16 technology clusters.
Unit: mention. An article naming several technologies contributes one mention per technology.

title: Appendix E. Supplementary Analyses to Analysis 3
text:
Journal Technology Mix

Method

Seven marketing journals: IJRM, JAMS, JCP, JCR, JM, JMR, MkSc.
Sample: empirical consumer-technology articles, 2000–2026, with a technology cluster assigned.
Unit: mention; an article naming several technologies contributes one mention per technology.
Counts cross-tabulated as journals (7) × technology clusters (16).


Deviation Test

Question: does a journal’s technology mix differ from the corpus as a whole?
Baseline b: overall technology cluster shares across the whole corpus, b_k = (Σ_j n_jk) / N.
Baseline includes the journal being tested, so all seven rows are read against one fixed reference point rather than seven shifting ones.
Validity: each mention falls in exactly one technology cluster, so a journal’s shares sum to 1 and the composition is proper; Dirichlet-multinomial applies.
Prior: Dirichlet, concentration α_k = K · b_k with K = 16 technology clusters, identical for every journal.
Prior mean = baseline, i.e. “this journal’s mix matches the corpus”.
Prior mass Σα_k = K, the same total weight as a flat Dirichlet(1, …, 1), redistributed proportionally rather than uniformly; equivalent to 16 pseudo-mentions of evidence for the null.
Effect: shrinks each journal toward the baseline, so small journals are pulled almost fully to the null and marks are harder to earn.
Posterior: Dirichlet-multinomial conjugacy, Dirichlet(α_k + n_jk) for journal j.
Sampling: gamma normalization, g_k ~ Gamma(α_k + n_jk, 1) then p_k = g_k / Σ g_k; 20,000 draws per journal, each a 16-vector summing to 1; single fixed seed.
Deviation per draw: d_k = p_k − b_k.
Interval: equal-tailed 95% credible interval, 2.5th and 97.5th percentile of the draws, read off the empirical quantiles.
Intervals marginal per cell, no multiplicity correction across the 7 × 16 cells.
Marks: ^1^ interval entirely above zero, ^2^ entirely below, blank spans zero.
Blank conflates no effect with too little data.
Marks concern share of a journal’s output, not counts; a small journal can be marked on modest absolute numbers.
Corpus is a census, so intervals generalize to the ongoing publishing process rather than to an unknown fixed quantity.




Results

Table 6 reports mentions per technology cluster and journal.
Rows are the 16 technology clusters, alphabetical with Other last; Total gives the cluster size across all seven journals.
Cell shares are row-wise, the share of the cluster’s mentions falling in that journal.
Marks are column-wise, on the journal’s own technology composition, so cell share and mark use different denominators.
^1^ a cluster credibly over-represented in that journal relative to its corpus-wide share, ^2^ credibly under-represented, blank no credible deviation.

Total gives the mentions of the technology cluster across all journals and its share of all mentions; the journal columns give the mentions of that cluster in the journal and its share of the cluster total. The marks are computed column-wise, on the journal’s own technology composition: 1 marks a technology cluster whose 95% credible interval lies entirely above its corpus-wide share, 2 one that lies entirely below it.

title: Appendix E. Supplementary Analyses to Analysis 3
text:
Introduction

This appendix documents how the corpus of consumer-technology research relates to itself and to the wider body of literature it draws on.
The corpus is the deduplicated set of academic articles used throughout the paper, each assigned to one of the 16 technology clusters.
Three perspectives are reported, each answering a different question about the same corpus:

Internal connectedness — does the corpus build on itself? Which technology clusters cite which other technology clusters, measured on direct citation links between articles inside the corpus.
Shared knowledge foundation — which references does the corpus build on in common? Measured on co-citation, that is, references that corpus articles cite together, described both by the co-citation clusters themselves and by the Scopus classification of the cited sources.
Bibliographic coupling — a more fine-grained view on the same question: which technology clusters draw on overlapping reference lists, measured on the number of references that pairs of corpus articles share.

All three perspectives use the same technology cluster assignment, so the 16 clusters are directly comparable across sections.
A fourth section reports the same citation network by journal rather than by technology cluster: which journals cite which.

title: Appendix E. Supplementary Analyses to Analysis 3
text:
Internal Connectedness

Method

Direct citation links were extracted with histNetwork() from the bibliometrix package, restricted to the 743 corpus articles, so that only citations from one corpus article to another corpus article are counted.
The network runs on one record per article, so an article is a single node regardless of how many technologies it names.
Cluster membership is assigned afterwards and kept multiple: an article naming technologies from several clusters belongs to each of them, and a tie between two such articles counts once per cluster pair it spans.
Every citation link was labelled with the technology cluster of the citing article and the technology cluster of the cited article.
Links were aggregated to the cluster level in both directions, giving two directed 16 × 16 grids:

cites — how many citations the row cluster makes to the column cluster.
cited by — how many citations the row cluster receives from the column cluster.

The diagonal reports citations within the row cluster itself.
Each cell carries a raw count, the cross-citation share \(CC_{ij}\) of row cluster \(i\) with column cluster \(j\), and the ratio \(r_{ij}\).
In the cites grid, \(CC_{ij}\) divides the cell by all citations the row cluster makes within the corpus: how its outgoing attention is distributed.
In the cited-by grid, \(CC_{ij}\) divides the cell by all citations the row cluster receives within the corpus: where its incoming attention comes from.
Rows sum to 100% in both grids, so \(CC_{ij}\) describes a cluster’s profile rather than its volume, and clusters of different size stay comparable.
\(\overline{CC}_j = \frac{1}{15}\sum_{i \neq j} CC_{ij}\), the average share the other clusters record for that same column cluster. eq j} CC_{ij}$, the average share the other clusters record for that same column cluster.
The average is taken over the fifteen other rows, excluding the column cluster’s own row, so a cluster’s internal citation does not set its own reference point.
\(r_{ij} = CC_{ij} / \overline{CC}_j\), so 1 = the usual amount of attention for that counterpart, 2 = twice as much, 0.5 = half.
On the diagonal, \(r_{ii}\) states how much more of its attention a cluster keeps internally than the other clusters direct at it.
\(CC_{ij}\) is read along a row, not down a column; the two grids are not transposes of one another, because they carry different denominators.
Code: 30_academic_foundation/07_citation_network.R; output: cites_by_table.csv / .md and cited_by_table.csv / .md.



Results

Figure 3 shows the direct citation network of the corpus, with articles coloured by technology cluster and edges running from citing to cited article.







Figure 3: Direct citation network within the corpus. Nodes are corpus articles, coloured by technology cluster; edges are citations from one corpus article to another.




Table 7 and Table 8 quantify the same structure as counts, \(CC_{ij}\) and \(r_{ij}\).
Rows and columns are labelled with the technology cluster name.
Reading a row of Table 7 gives how one technology cluster spreads its citations, reading the same row of Table 8 gives where its citations come from.
Comparing the two tables cell by cell gives the direction of the relationship between two clusters.
The diagonal \(CC_{ii}\) states how much of a cluster’s citing, and of its being cited, stays inside the cluster.





Table 7: How the citations each technology cluster makes are distributed across the clusters. Cells report the number of citations the row cluster \(i\) makes to the column cluster \(j\), the cross-citation share \(CC_{ij}\) of all citations \(i\) makes within the corpus, and the ratio \(r_{ij} = CC_{ij} / \overline{CC}_j\), where \(\overline{CC}_j\) is the average share the fifteen other clusters direct at \(j\). A ratio of 1 means the row cluster gives the column cluster its usual amount of attention and 2 twice as much. Rows sum to 100%. The diagonal reports citations within the row cluster itself.

Co-Mention Within the Same Article

A measure of connectedness that does not rely on citations, reported alongside the citation grids because it answers the same question from the other side.
Unit: article. For every pair of technology clusters, the number of corpus articles that name a technology from both.
An article mentioning several technologies of the same cluster counts once for that cluster, so the cell counts articles rather than mentions.
The matrix is symmetric and the diagonal is empty, because a cluster cannot co-occur with itself.
The final column sums the row and therefore counts co-occurrence links rather than articles: an article naming three clusters contributes two to each of those clusters.
The cross-mention rate is the share of a cluster’s own articles that also mention a technology from another cluster, counting each article once, and is therefore not affected by the size of the cluster.
Read against the citation grids above, a cluster can be strongly self-citing yet frequently co-mentioned, or the reverse, because the two measures track different behaviours.

title: Appendix E. Supplementary Analyses to Analysis 3
text:
Shared Knowledge Foundation

Method

Co-citation counts how often two references are cited together by the same corpus article, which identifies the bodies of work the corpus builds on in common, including references outside the corpus.
Before clustering, the most cited references were screened by hand and pure method papers, that is, references concerned solely with a method and not with its application to any topic, were removed.
The co-citation network was built with biblioNetwork(analysis = "co-citation", network = "references") on the deduplicated corpus and drawn with networkPlot() using a Fruchterman-Reingold layout, the 500 most cited references, a minimum edge weight of 3, Louvain community detection, a community repulsion of 0.8, and a fixed seed.
The same network is reported from two perspectives, so the nodes and edges are identical in both and only the colouring differs:

Louvain co-citation clusters — the communities the algorithm itself finds in the co-citation network, that is, groups of references that are habitually cited together.
Scopus classification of the cited sources — each cited reference matched to its source journal in the Scopus source list and labelled with the 4 Scopus top-level fields and the Scopus broad subject areas of that source.

For the second perspective, a reference was counted once per article and field, so an article citing several sources from the same field contributes once.
In the custom rendering, each reference node is additionally coloured by the technology cluster that dominates its citing articles, using a dominance threshold of 0.25; nodes below the threshold are labelled as having no dominant cluster.
Deviation test for the Louvain base clusters, same procedure as the journal test in Appendix B:

Unit: matched article-reference mention; one reference belongs to exactly one base cluster.
Counts: technology clusters (16) × base clusters; cell = mentions of that cluster in that base cluster.
Baseline b: overall base cluster shares across all technology clusters, column sums over the whole table.
Validity: categories mutually exclusive and exhaustive, row shares sum to 1, so the composition is proper and Dirichlet-multinomial applies.
Prior: Dirichlet, concentration α = b × number of base clusters, identical for every technology cluster.
Prior mean = baseline, i.e. “this cluster’s reference mix matches the corpus”.
Prior mass = number of base clusters, the same total weight as a flat Dirichlet(1, …, 1), redistributed proportionally; as uninformative as the flat prior, shrinking small clusters toward the baseline.
Posterior: Dirichlet-multinomial conjugacy, Dirichlet(α + row counts).
Sampling: gamma normalization, 20,000 draws per technology cluster, each a full vector summing to 1; fixed seed.
Deviation per draw: d = posterior share − baseline share.
Interval: equal-tailed 95% credible interval, 2.5th and 97.5th percentile of the draws.
Marks: ^1^ interval entirely above zero, ^2^ entirely below, blank spans zero.
Intervals marginal per cell, no multiplicity correction.
Not applied to the Scopus tables: an article can cite several fields, rows do not sum to 1, so the composition is not proper.
Mentions within one article are correlated, so the effective sample size is below the mention count and the intervals are narrower than the paper-level evidence warrants.

title: Appendix E. Supplementary Analyses to Analysis 3
text:
Bibliographic Coupling

Method

Bibliographic coupling counts how many references two corpus articles share, so it measures overlap in reference lists directly at the level of article pairs rather than at the level of reference communities.
It is reported here as a more fine-grained view on the Louvain co-citation clusters of the previous section: co-citation groups references that are cited together, whereas coupling states, for each pair of technology clusters, how much of their reference base is literally the same.
The coupling network was built with biblioNetwork(analysis = "coupling", network = "references") on the deduplicated corpus.
All unique article pairs were extracted from the coupling matrix and labelled with the technology cluster of both articles.
Pairs with no shared reference were retained, so that clusters of different size remain comparable.
The reported statistic is the mean coupling strength: the average number of shared references across all possible article pairs of the row and the column cluster.
The diagonal reports pairs of articles inside the same technology cluster.
Code: 30_academic_foundation/05_bibliographic_coupling.R; output: cluster_coupling_matrix.csv and cluster_coupling_matrix.md.



Results

Table 14 reports the mean coupling strength for all 16 × 16 cluster combinations.
Row labels carry the cluster number and the cluster name; column headers carry the cluster number only.
The matrix is symmetric, because coupling is undirected.
Higher values indicate that a randomly drawn article pair from the two clusters shares more references; a value of 0 indicates that no article pair between the two clusters shares any reference.
Comparing a diagonal cell to the remainder of its row gives the balance between reference overlap inside and outside the own technology cluster.





Table 14: Mean bibliographic coupling strength between technology clusters. Cells report the average number of shared references across all possible paper pairs of the row and column cluster, including pairs with no shared reference. Columns are numbered as in the row labels.

title: Appendix E. Supplementary Analyses to Analysis 3
text:
Journal-Level View

Method

Same within-corpus citation network as above, aggregated to journals instead of technology clusters.
Directed 7 × 7 grid; cells report cited by / cites.
Diagonal reports within-journal citations, where both numbers would describe the same links.
Deviation test on the same grid, same procedure as the technology mix test in Appendix B.
Run twice, once on the citations a journal makes and once on the citations it receives, because the two carry different denominators.
Diagonal excluded and each row renormalised over the six other journals, so the test asks where a journal directs its outward attention rather than how much it cites itself.
Baseline: the pooled distribution of off-diagonal citations across the seven journals, one fixed reference point for all rows.
Prior: Dirichlet, concentration α_k = 6 · b_k, prior mean = baseline, so small journals are pulled toward the null.
Posterior: 20,000 draws per journal, equal-tailed 95% credible interval on the deviation from the baseline.
Intervals marginal per cell, no multiplicity correction across the 42 off-diagonal cells of each grid.
Marks: ^1^ interval entirely above zero, ^2^ entirely below, blank spans zero.
The mark on the first number of a cell concerns the column journal’s citing profile, the mark on the second the row journal’s.
Code: 30_academic_foundation/08_journal_technology_bayes.R and 30_academic_foundation/07_citation_network.R.
Output: figure_journals.png, journal_citation_matrix_marked.csv / .md.



Results

Figure 6 shows the within-corpus citation network with articles arranged by journal.







Figure 6: Direct citation network within the corpus, with articles arranged by journal. Nodes are corpus articles, coloured by technology cluster; edges are citations from one corpus article to another.




Table 15 quantifies that network.
Reading a row gives, for one journal, how often each other journal cites it and how often it cites each other journal.
Comparing the two numbers in a cell gives the direction of the relationship between the two journals.





Table 15: Direct citation links between the seven journals within the corpus, with the deviation test. Cells report cited by / cites: the number of citations the column journal makes to the row journal, and the number of citations the row journal makes to the column journal. The diagonal describes within-journal citations and is excluded from the test. Marks come from Dirichlet posteriors on each journal’s citation profile over the six other journals, against the pooled distribution across all journals as the baseline: 1 a share whose 95% credible interval lies entirely above the baseline share, 2 one that lies entirely below it, blank no credible deviation. The mark on the first number concerns the column journal’s citing profile, the mark on the second the row journal’s.

title: Appendix E. Supplementary Analyses to Analysis 3
text:
Introduction

Two questions on what predicts how often a corpus paper is cited.
Early adoption: does entering a technology cluster early pay off?
Citation breadth: does citing within one’s own cluster or across clusters pay off?
Each estimated overall, across all 16 technology clusters, and separately per cluster.
Descriptive and observational; no causal identification.

title: Appendix E. Supplementary Analyses to Analysis 3
text:
Shared Setup

Method

Sample: corpus papers present in the within-corpus citation network, each with a technology cluster and a publication year.
Two outcomes, reported side by side:

Within Corpus — local citations, citations received from other corpus articles.
Total — global citations, citations received from anywhere.

Model family: negative-binomial GAM (mgcv::gam, family = nb()), appropriate for over-dispersed counts.
Publication age (age = 2026 − PY) entered as a smooth, so no decay shape is assumed.
Age is discrete; the basis dimension is capped below the number of distinct ages available.
Overall models additionally control for cluster citeability, the mean global citations of the paper’s cluster.
Per-cluster models omit that control, since it is constant within a cluster.
Coefficients are on the log scale of the expected citation count.
Code: 30_academic_foundation/07_citation_network.R.

title: Appendix E. Supplementary Analyses to Analysis 3
text:
Early Adoption

Method

Predictor: early adoption score = publication year − year of the earliest paper in the same technology cluster.
Lower score = earlier entry into the cluster; 0 = the cluster’s first paper.
Negative coefficient = earlier papers accumulate more citations.
Overall specification: citations ~ early adoption score + cluster citeability + s(age).
Per-cluster specification: citations ~ early adoption score, fitted separately for each of the 16 clusters.
Output: impact_early_adoption_per_cluster.csv / .md.



Results

Overall, across all 16 technology clusters:

Within Corpus: [coefficient and p-value to be added]
Total: [coefficient and p-value to be added]

Table 16 reports the same model fitted separately per cluster.
Rows are the 16 technology clusters; cells give the coefficient with its p-value in parentheses.
Sign indicates direction: negative = earlier papers more cited, positive = later papers more cited.
Per-cluster estimates rest on the papers of that cluster only, so small clusters give less precise estimates.

section: Citing Within and Across Technology Clusters
text:
Citing Within and Across Technology Clusters

Method

Two predictors, both counted on citations the paper makes, not receives:

wi — citations to papers of its own technology cluster.
ac — citations to papers of other technology clusters.

Both standardised by opportunity, since early papers have fewer papers available to cite:

wi divided by the papers published in the same cluster before that year.
ac divided by the papers published in all other clusters before that year.

Papers with an undefined standardised score, that is no prior papers to cite, are dropped.
Overall specification: citations ~ wi + ac + cluster citeability + s(age).
Per-cluster specification: citations ~ wi + ac + s(age), fitted separately for each of the 16 clusters.

title: Appendix E. Supplementary Analyses to Analysis 3
text:
Search Construction
For each of the 901 canonical technologies, we generated a title-restricted Media Cloud query and a corresponding Python regular expression using gpt-4.1-mini through the OpenAI API (\(T = 0\); JSON-schema-constrained structured output). Queries consist of wildcard-prefixed terms joined with AND and OR operators, restricted to article titles with the article_title:(...) syntax.
Media Cloud’s title-search operator does not enforce word adjacency or word order, so the query alone returns titles in which the constituent words appear anywhere in any order. We therefore applied the regular expression locally to every retrieved title, requiring the constituent words of the technology term to occur directly next to one another and in the intended order. Titles that did not satisfy the regular expression were discarded as false positives.
Searches ran against the United States – National collection (collection ID 34412234) and covered January 1, 2000, through June 30, 2026. Duplicate stories within a technology were removed. A story matching more than one technology was retained once per technology, mirroring the treatment of multi-technology articles in Study 1. Retained records were stored per technology term and combined into an annual cluster-level series. The full set of search strings and regular expressions is reported in Table 18.

title: Appendix E. Supplementary Analyses to Analysis 3
section: Rank-Order Agreement Between the Two Corpora
text:
Rank-Order Agreement Between the Two Corpora
The cross-sectional comparison in the main text contrasts the attention shares themselves. This section reports the same contrast on the ordering of the clusters alone, which asks whether the two corpora agree on which technologies matter most, irrespective of how much attention separates them. Each cluster is ranked within each corpus on its pooled share over the whole period, with rank 1 the cluster holding the largest share, and the two orderings are compared with Spearman’s \(\rho\) and Kendall’s \(\tau\). Ties are averaged. As with the \(G\) test, both corpora are censuses of their retrieval frames rather than random samples, so the \(p\)-values quantify the discrepancy against the null of no rank association rather than sampling error.
The two orderings agree moderately, \(\rho = .634\), \(p = .008\), \(\tau = .494\), \(p = .008\), with a mean absolute rank difference of 3.1 positions across the sixteen clusters. Generative AI carries the largest positive difference, ranking first in the academic corpus against eighth in the media corpus, followed by Gaming & Digital Platforms and Algorithms & Recommendations at six positions each. The largest negative differences are Other and Internet & Broadcasting, which the media corpus ranks third and second against tenth and joint seventh in the academic corpus. Two clusters occupy the same rank in both corpora, Computers & Software at five and Auctions & Pricing at sixteen. Table 19 reports all clusters.
Ranks depend only on the ordering of the pooled counts within each corpus, and both attention bases divide those counts by a denominator that is constant across clusters. The rank order, the rank differences and the two coefficients are therefore identical on the within-technology and the overall basis, and Table 23 reproduces Table 19 for completeness with the shares restated on the overall basis.




Table 19: Rank order of the technology clusters in the academic and the media corpus, 2008–2026. Academic share and media share are the pooled share of attention that each cluster received within all consumer-technology mentions of its respective corpus, pooled across the whole period rather than averaged over years. Ranks are assigned on those shares, with 1 the cluster holding the largest share of its corpus. The rank difference is the media rank minus the academic rank, so positive values indicate a cluster the field ranks higher than the public does and negative values the reverse. Across the 16 clusters the two orderings agree at \(\rho = .634\) (\(p = .008\)) and \(\tau = .494\) (\(p = .008\)), with a mean absolute rank difference of 3.1 positions and a maximum of 7. Half ranks indicate ties.

section: Journal-Level Comparison with the Media Benchmark
text:
Journal-Level Comparison with the Media Benchmark
The comparisons above treat the academic corpus as one body. This section splits it by outlet and asks the same two questions of each of the seven journals separately: how its allocation of attention across the sixteen clusters departs from the media allocation, and how closely its attention peaks track the media peaks. Both use the 2008–2026 window and the within-technology basis. Denominators are the journal’s own technology mentions, so a journal is compared with the media benchmark and not with the other journals.

Attention Gap by Journal
Table 20 reports one row per cluster, with an Overall column for the pooled corpus and one column per journal. Each cell gives the academic minus media share in percentage points, the media rank minus the academic rank in parentheses, and stars for the Benjamini-Hochberg corrected binomial \(q\)-value computed across the sixteen clusters within that column.
The direction of the field-level gaps is shared by nearly every journal. Generative AI is over-covered in all seven, from \(+3.5\) percentage points in Journal of Marketing Research to \(+17.8\) in Journal of Consumer Psychology, and Internet & Broadcasting is under-covered in all seven, between \(-8.4\) and \(-14.8\) points. Algorithms & Recommendations is over-covered in all seven and Social Media under-covered in all seven. Departures from the shared pattern are few: Search & Advertising is under-covered everywhere except Marketing Science, where it is over-covered by \(3.0\) points, and Computers & Software is under-covered everywhere except Journal of Consumer Research.




Table 20: Attention gap per technology cluster, overall and by journal, 2008-2026. Each cell gives the academic minus media share in percentage points and, in parentheses, the media rank minus the academic rank; positive values mark clusters covered more than the media covers them. Stars mark the Benjamini-Hochberg corrected binomial q-value: * q < .05, ** q < .01, *** q < .001. In this table, q means: if this journal had allocated its articles across the 16 technologies in exactly the proportions the media did, how often would you see a gap this large in this cluster by chance alone?

Peak-Year Agreement
The gap table is cross-sectional and says nothing about timing. For each cluster we therefore took the year of maximum attention in the media and the year of maximum attention in each journal, both on a three-year rolling average of the within-technology share, and correlated the two orderings across clusters with Spearman’s \(\rho\) and Kendall’s \(\tau\). Only the ordering enters, so a journal scores high if it reaches its maximum on the technologies the media peaked on early before those the media peaked on late, whatever the size of its attention. Clusters a journal never published on are dropped, which leaves fourteen or fifteen clusters for three of the journals. Table 21 reports the peak years themselves and Table 22 the agreement.
Agreement is weak throughout. Journal of Marketing Research is closest at \(\rho = .450\), followed by Journal of Consumer Research, Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science and Marketing Science between \(.368\) and \(.385\); International Journal of Research in Marketing reaches \(.134\), and Journal of Marketing and Journal of Consumer Psychology sit at zero or below. Median year differences are small and of both signs, from \(-5\) years for Journal of Marketing to \(+1\) year for Journal of Consumer Research and International Journal of Research in Marketing.
Two features of Table 21 limit how far these coefficients can be read. Clusters whose attention was still rising in 2026 peak at the window edge in both series by construction, which raises agreement for every journal alike, and clusters a journal covered with only one or two articles place their peak wherever those articles fall.

title: Appendix E. Supplementary Analyses to Analysis 3
text:
Robustness Check: Overall Attention Basis
The main manuscript reports attention shares computed within technology-related output only, so that each cluster’s share is measured against the other fifteen clusters. As a robustness check, we recomputed both analyses on an overall basis, in which each cluster’s share is measured against all publications and all newspaper articles of the period, whether technology-related or not. Shares are pooled across the whole period rather than averaged over years, on both bases. The two bases differ only in their denominator; the underlying counts are identical.

Cross-Sectional Comparison
We applied the same procedure as in the main text. The \(G\) test requires the reference proportions to sum to one, so the overall basis adds a residual “not tech-related” category to the sixteen clusters, giving 17 categories and \(n = 7{,}864\) academic publications.
On this basis, the distribution of academic publications departs from the corresponding media proportions, \(G(16) = 2153.96\), \(p < .001\), \(w = .52\), with a total variation distance of \(.11\). Fifteen of the sixteen clusters hold a larger share of academic than of media attention and one holds a smaller share. The ratio of academic to media share ranges from \(1.00\) for Internet & Broadcasting to \(153.66\) for Auctions & Pricing. Fifteen cluster-level tests remain significant after correction; Internet & Broadcasting does not (\(q = 1.00\)).

title: Appendix E. Supplementary Analyses to Analysis 3
section: Permutation Tests of the Lag Correlations
text:
Permutation Tests of the Lag Correlations
The cross-correlations reported in the main text are descriptive. Here we attach an exact permutation test to each of them, on both the within-technology basis used in the main text and the overall basis used in the robustness check. A conventional Pearson test does not apply to these series, because annual attention shares are autocorrelated and the observations are therefore not independent.
For each lag, we first aligned the two series at that lag and then shifted the media series circularly against the academic series. A circular shift moves every observation forward by the same offset and wraps the end of the series back to the start, which preserves the internal order and autocorrelation of the media series while breaking its alignment with the academic series. Aligning before shifting keeps the circular shift from being confounded with the lag itself. The \(p\)-value is two-sided,
\[
p = \frac{1 + \#\{\text{shifted correlations with } |r| \geq |r_{\text{obs}}|\}}{1 + \text{number of shifts}},
\]
and we enumerated every available shift rather than sampling from them, which makes the test exact and removes any dependence on a random seed.
Enumeration also fixes the resolution of the test. A series of \(n\) observations admits exactly \(n\) circular shifts, one of which is the identity, so the smallest attainable \(p\)-value is \(1/n\). Aligning at lag \(L\) reduces the overlap to \(19 - |L|\) years, and the number of available shifts equals that overlap. The lower bound therefore depends on the lag: \(1/19 = .053\) at lag 0, rising to \(1/14 = .071\) at lags \(-5\) and \(+5\). No cell in either table can fall below \(.05\), and drawing more permutations than the number of available shifts does not lower this bound, because additional draws only repeat the same arrangements.
The within-technology basis is reported in the main manuscript and Table 24 reports the overall basis, each giving the correlation at every lag with its \(p\)-value in parentheses and the highest correlation in each row set in bold.
On the within-technology basis, the smallest values occur for Generative AI and Search & Advertising, which sit at the per-lag lower bound across a contiguous run of lags. All remaining values lie above \(.05\).
On the overall basis, Generative AI sits at the lower bound at every lag, and Gaming & Digital Platforms and Streaming, Audio & Video sit at or near it across the positive lags. All remaining values lie above \(.05\).

title: Mapping the Field
text:
Over the past quarter-century, marketing and consumer research has shown increased interest and publication output in new consumer technologies (Hoffman et al., 2022), with Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) the latest in line. Generative AI has permeated many aspects of individuals’, marketers’, and researchers’ experience with an unprecedented impact and at a rapid pace (Cillo & Rubera, 2025; Grewal et al., 2025; C. L. Wang, 2026). Demonstrating rapid adoption rates (Hu & Hu, 2023; Semrush, 2026) and implementation proliferation across many technologies and processes (Cillo & Rubera, 2025; Grewal et al., 2025), it is unsurprising that this new consumer technology is salient in both business and academic discourse (Bart et al., 2026; Kennedy et al., 2025; C. L. Wang, 2026). At the same time, critical voices warn that the “AI hype” is not a revolution, but merely the next step in technological evolution (Moschella, 2025; Zachary, 2026). While other work discusses how Generative AI disrupts patterns in consumers’ usage of technologies (Mogaji & Jain, 2024), or marketers’ approach to integrating new technologies into their business (Cillo & Rubera, 2025), in this paper we turn the perspective towards ourselves as researchers in the domain of consumer technology research, and ask: Is Generative AI as a new consumer technology different from what our field has studied before? As such, in this paper, we treat Generative AI not as the technology it is, but as the knowledge phenomenon claiming its place in our field of consumer technology research. 
We consider the answer to this question consequential on three grounds: First, researchers in marketing and consumer research can have substantive impact on consumer wellbeing, policymaking and regulations (de Bellis et al., 2026; Kaltenbrunner, 2020). Generative AI has undoubtedly had a profound impact in a relatively short amount of time, warranting the attention devoted to it by both academics and the public. Yet we must ask whether this comes at a cost: the attention we can devote as a field is limited due to factors such as the publishing and review process (Björk & Solomon, 2013; Ellison, 2002), funding (Fabbri et al., 2018; Kaltenbrunner, 2020), and, ultimately, the researchers’ time. The question is therefore not only how much attention we pay to Generative AI, but also what other topics forgo attention as a result. We therefore ask: How does our field allocate attention to consumer technologies, and does Generative AI disrupt these patterns?
Second, research on consumer technologies is fast-paced and evolves as fast as the technologies themselves (Hoffman et al., 2022; Malter et al., 2020). To produce scientific output that is relevant, we must focus on the essence of these technologies (de Bellis et al., 2026), and we must build a scientific agenda that is cumulative instead of isolated to be able to keep up, but also to understand the fundamental similarities and differences between many fast-paced iterations within and across technologies (de Bellis et al., 2026; Malter et al., 2020). Especially with a technology such as Generative AI, we must carefully investigate our field’s response, as its adoption and proliferation happen at unprecedented speed (Grewal et al., 2025; Semrush, 2026). Without relying on what we already know, we will not be able to build a cumulative understanding of what is to come, limiting our ability to offer value to consumers and policymakers (point 1). We therefore ask: How does our field connect its research within and across technologies, what theories do we build on, and does Generative AI demonstrate a different type of connectedness than earlier technologies?
Third, research does not happen in isolation. The attention we devote to consumer technologies must match the importance given to these technologies by the public at least to a certain extent, as our research has value to offer, and we must direct our limited attention to the areas that matter to the public [some sources]. In the context of Generative AI, it is easy to assume that it is all consumers talk about. But is this truly the case, and if not, what else has mattered in the past, and matters now in the current landscape of consumer technologies? Understanding where the public puts its attention may also help us understand if the cost we pay to study Generative AI (point 1) is justified. We therefore ask: How strongly is our research agenda influenced by what matters to the public, and is it different for Generative AI?
Understanding how Generative AI compares to earlier consumer technologies is relevant for stakeholders across the scientific ecosystem: Journals are influential in how they set their agendas, and therefore substantively shape where researchers put their attention. Researchers, on the other hand, are motivated both by what type of research is called for in journals and by what calls for attention in the public domain. At the same time, demands for innovation and novelty may disincentivize research on so-called hype topics [sources]. Lastly, institutions and funding bodies are called to allocate resources to research that has impact and matters to the public, but also to ensure that our field advances cumulatively rather than through many isolated streams of research, missing out on vital learnings from each other.
All of our questions are inherently comparative, and cannot be answered by looking at Generative AI in isolation. Consequently, in this paper, we follow two objectives: First, we aim to build a comprehensive overview of how consumer technology research has evolved at large, understanding diffusion patterns of attention to individual consumer technologies, the research domain’s intellectual foundation and interconnectedness, and how academic attention towards consumer technologies tracks public salience. Second, we aim to use this overview as a baseline and contrast it with the case of Generative AI across all three dimensions. As we argue that journals play a major role in how a research agenda evolves, we additionally aim to understand the influence of individual leading marketing journals on the trajectory of consumer technology research as a whole, and the case of Generative AI specifically.
This paper contributes to the understanding of our field in three ways. While several studies demonstrate the speed and breadth of publications on Generative AI (Raman et al., 2024; Riandhi et al., 2025), to the best of our knowledge there is currently no study systematically comparing our field’s response to Generative AI with its response to earlier technologies. We address this by building an overview of a quarter-century of empirical consumer technology research in marketing and classifying consumer technologies into clusters, which gives us a baseline against which we can compare the reaction to Generative AI with the reaction to previous technology clusters (Analysis 1). Second, we conduct a bibliometric analysis on this overview, showing how connected our field is within and across research on specific clusters of consumer technologies, and which theoretical foundations it builds on. Our corpus covers 26 years of consumer technology research, which allows us to say where the reaction to Generative AI falls within the established connectedness and theoretical foundation of our field, and where it breaks out (Analysis 2). Due to our bottom-up corpus generation, our analysis and implications are not constrained by top-down, a priori defined inclusion criteria typical for bibliometric analyses, letting us locate Generative AI within the field’s established patterns of connectedness empirically. Lastly, we extend our perspective from looking within our field to looking at the public salience of the consumer technologies we study, using media mentions as a proxy. Because both are built on the same semantic basis, academic and public attention can be contrasted directly. This allows us to show, for the first time, where our field’s agenda aligns with public salience and where it diverges, and how Generative AI breaks with the historical pattern (Analysis 3).

title: Mapping the Field
text:
Inclusion and Exclusion of Articles
Using SCOPUS and Web of Science, we collect all papers published between January 1st, 2000 and June 30th, 2026 in the seven leading marketing journals Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science (JAMS), Journal of Consumer Psychology (JCP), Journal of Consumer Research (JCR), Journal of Marketing (JM), Journal of Marketing Research (JMR), Marketing Science (MS), and the International Journal of Research in Marketing (IJRM). Merging and deduplicating the two databases with the bibliometrix package (Aria & Cuccurullo, 2017), we identify \(10,140\) unique articles. We screen every article on its indexed title and abstract with a two-stage LLM pipeline (GPT-4.1-mini, temperature = 0, JSON outputs), using a positive-worded prompt in the first pass (“Does this article discuss a technology?”) and a negative-worded prompt in the second (“Does this article not discuss a technology?”), with the LLM listing all technologies where an article discusses several. A human rater validates every article on which the two passes disagree and we carry the human decision forward, retaining \(1,762\) articles mentioning \(2,713\) technologies. A third prompt with the same configuration classifies each candidate technology on whether it is consumer-facing and whether the study is empirical; a human rater evaluates a random 20% of titles and abstracts, with 91% agreement. The final inclusion produces \(1,583\) technology mentions in \(1,155\) empirical articles. Figure 1 describes the full inclusion and exclusion pipeline. Following Hoffman et al. (2022), we define new [consumer] technologies as “scientific knowledge and/or its application in the early adoption cycle for firms and/or consumers with the potential to influence the activity, institutions, and processes for creating, communicating, delivering, and exchanging offerings that have value for customers, clients, partners, and society at large”. These technologies have changed the world of consumers and firms, but also how we as researchers operate within this space.






Figure 1: Inclusion and exclusion pipeline. \(n_\text{articles}\) describes the number of articles included in the respective steps, \(n_\text{articles+}\) describes the number of articles fitting the positive inclusion criterion, \(n_\text{articles-}\) describes the number of articles fitting the negative exclusion criterion (no technology). \(n_\text{tech-mentions}\) describes the number of technology mentions for each step, as one article can mention more than one technology in its title and abstract.

title: Mapping the Field
text:
Semantic Deduplication and Clustering
We clean and standardize the \(1,583\) mentions by lowercasing them, removing abbreviations, hyphens, slashes, and other special characters, and singularizing them, and then deduplicate them semantically on pairwise cosine similarities derived from all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019; Sentence Transformers, 2026; W. Wang et al., 2020), collapsing any pair with a cosine similarity \(\geq .90\) and retaining the most central term as the canonical technology label. We reduce the 384 embedding dimensions with UMAP on cosine distance, 15 neighbors and a minimum distance of 0 (McInnes et al., 2018), testing UMAP dimensions between 2 and 50 and deduplication thresholds between 0.90 and 0.95, and aggregate the embeddings into clusters with k-means (MacQueen, 1967), testing solutions between 10 and 20 clusters. We select the final configuration on a systematic comparison of trustworthiness scores for the dimensionality reduction (Venna & Kaski, 2001), Silhouette (Rousseeuw, 1987), Davies-Bouldin (Davies & Bouldin, 1979) and Calinski-Harabasz scores (Caliński & Harabasz, 1974), inertia (MacQueen, 1967), and the human interpretability of the resulting clusters, which we then check and label manually.

title: Mapping the Field
text:
Bibliometric Analysis
Using the bibliometrix package (Aria & Cuccurullo, 2017), we assess the interconnectedness of the sixteen technology clusters with historiographic plots (histplot) and co-citation analyses (biblionetwork) using Louvain clustering algorithms.
The historiographic analysis is a chronolgical network analysis and map of citations within a bibliographic collection (Aria & Cuccurullo, 2017; Garfield, 2004). We aggregate citation ties per direction (forward citations: articles being cited by later articles in the corpus; and backward citations: articles citing earlier articles in the corpus) within and across clusters on a technology cluster mention level, meaning that articles discussing several technology clusters are counted once under each of them. We assess how frequently different technology clusters co-occur within the same article, and we compare the cross-citation links \(\text{CC}_{\text{Cluster}_i,\text{Cluster}_j} = \frac{\text{Links}_{ij}}{\sum_{k=1}^{16}\text{Links}_{ik}}\) that is, the share of cluster \(i\)’s links that go to cluster \(j\), against the share that all other clusters direct at \(j\) on average (\(\overline{\text{CC}}_{\text{Cluster}_j}=\frac{1}{15}\sum_{i \neq j}\text{CC}_{ij}\)). The ratio \(r_{ij} = \frac{CC_{ij}}{\overline{CC}_{j}}\) then states whether the links between cluster \(i\) and \(j\) are stronger (\(r > 1\)), about as strong (\(r = 1\)), or weaker (\(r < 1\)) than expected across the full corpus.
We further analyse the co-citations among the references cited by the articles in our corpus. Two references are co-cited when a third article cites both (Aria & Cuccurullo, 2017, p. 969). Its primary purpose is to map the intellectual foundations of a corpus, as references that are frequently cited together are interpreted as evidence of shared themes underlying the corpus (Small, 1980). Before clustering, we manually screened the most cited references and removed pure method papers, that is, references concerned solely with a method and not with its application to any topic. We analyze the 500 most cited references across our corpus of consumer technology research, applying Louvain community detection with a minimum edge weight of 3 and a community repulsion of 0.8 using the bibliometrix package (Aria & Cuccurullo, 2017), and label the resulting communities by hand using the shared themes of their ten most cited references. We map each cluster’s references onto these foundations and compute the share of its references falling into each base for each of the sixteen clusters and for the corpus as a whole. For every cluster we then estimate a Dirichlet posterior over its share vector (Andrew, 2010), using the overall corpus distribution as the prior, and treat a foundation as diverging from the corpus when the cluster’s 95% credible interval excludes the overall share of that foundation.
In the Supplementary Materials, we provide additional bibliometric perspectives by computing bibliographic coupling metrics, and analyze the academic fields referenced by the consumer technology corpus using Scopus’ top-level field and broad subject area classification of the cited sources.

title: Mapping the Field
text:
Media Benchmark
To understand what matters to the beneficiaries of our research, we need to understand what the public devotes its attention to. Media presence influences what consumers think about, and in turn is influenced by what matters to consumers, i.e. what gets read (Scheufele, 1999). We construct a proxy for public attention using media stories on consumer technologies relying on MediaCloud, an open source collection of global news on the open web (Roberts et al., 2021). For our analysis, we use the US News collection (ID: 34412234) indexing 247 US news sources (Bermejo et al., 2026). We transform every consumer technology identified in our academic corpus (\(n = 901\)) into a regular-expression search query using wildcards and spelling alternatives, and query the MediaCloud API on all media story titles queried since 20081. We are interested in which consumer technologies hold focal attention in consumer’s minds, which is why we search for mentions of these technologies in the indexed story titles. We count the number of stories mentioning each consumer technology, removing duplicate-stories within technologies, and aggregate the counts to the clusters identified through semantic modeling.
We then compare the share of attention devoted to each technology cluster in academic articles and media stories over the entire period from January 1st, 2008 until June 30th, 2026, by counting the mentions of that cluster across the whole period and dividing by the total number of hits across all sixteen clusters. We treat the media shares as the baseline and test whether the share of academic attention devoted to each cluster credibly diverges from it, using Dirichlet posteriors (Andrew, 2010) with the media distribution as the prior. For each cluster we compute the ratio of its academic to its media share, and treat a cluster as diverging when the ratio’s 95% credible interval excludes 1, i.e. is credibly higher (\(r > 1\)) or credibly lower (\(r < 1\)) than the media representation.
We compare the temporal trajectory of academic and media attention by correlating the annual academic and media share at lags ranging from \(-5\) years (share of academic attention prior to media attention) to \(+5\) years (share of academic attention following media attention), with \(0\) as concurrent attention. Because annual attention shares are autocorrelated, conventional tests of these correlations do not apply, and we instead compute an exact two-sided permutation test that shifts the media series circularly against the academic series, enumerating every available shift. The procedure is described in full in Appendix E. At 19 lags, p-values for each permutation can range from \(.053\) at lag \(0\) to \(.071\) at the boundary lags, the tests are therefore only limitedly informative.

title: Mapping the Field
section: Analysis 1. Modeling 26 years of consumer technology research
text:
Analysis 1. Modeling 26 years of consumer technology research
In Analysis 1, we pursue two goals: First, we semantically map a quarter-century of consumer technology research. We treat the language authors use to describe a technology as an indicator for its relatedness to other technologies, closer semantic similarity indicating closer relatedness. Second, we trace the resulting clusters of consumer technologies over time.

The field at large
Using embeddings derived from all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019; Sentence Transformers, 2026; W. Wang et al., 2020), a similarity score of 0.90, 10 UMAP dimensions, and 16 clusters, the semantic deduplication reduced the \(1,583\) consumer technologies to \(901\) unique consumer technologies. Our final model produces a trustworthiness of \(.924\), a silhouette score of \(.436\), a Davies-Bouldin score of \(.920\), a Calinski-Harabasz score of \(459.45\), and an inertia of \(421.49\). This model produced the best tradeoff between statistical adequacy and human interpretability, and we therefore carried it forward for all further analyses. We report all comparisons, including additional semantic models we tested against all-MiniLM-L6-v2, in Appendix A. We manually analyzed and labeled every cluster, resulting in 16 final clusters, of which 15 had a clearly identifiable theme, and one cluster was labeled as Other to summarize miscellaneous technologies. All clusters are listed in Table 1 and visualized in Figure 2.






Figure 2: Semantic map visualizing all 901 technologies through further reduction of 10 UMAP dimensions to two. Colors indicate the assignment to the respective clusters.



Across the seven journals, we compare each journal’s focus on a technology cluster against the corpus-wide focus on that cluster, using Dirichlet posteriors with the overall distribution as the prior. Journal profiles are largely in line with the corpus, but some patterns emerge. MS dominates discussions of pricing and channel problems, holding credibly more than its expected share of Auctions & Pricing (46%), Streaming, Audio & Video (37%) and E-Commerce (33%). IJRM dominates technologies early in their adoption and diffusion cycle, credibly over-represented in Crypto & Fintech (31%) and, descriptively though not credibly, in Generative AI (21%), but also credibly in Smartphones & Apps (26%). Systematic under-representation is rarer; the clearest case is JCP, which falls credibly below its expected share for Gaming & Digital Platforms, Social Media, and Streaming, Audio & Video. Detailed results are reported in the Appendix B.
The share of technologies across time shows that empirical research discussing consumer technologies increased sharply from 2014 onwards, and received another wave of attention from 2022 onwards (Figure 3 Panel A). Computers & Software and Internet & Broadcasting dominate early consumer technology research, give way to a strong focus on Smartphones, and shortly after also Social Media, which in turn are replaced by Generative AI from approximately 2022 onwards (Figure 3 Panel B). The peak years corroborate these patterns statistically: Computers & Software and Internet & Broadcasting peak in 2000, the year in which they take up their comparatively largest share, and decline continuously thereafter (\(p < .001\)), whereas Smartphones & Apps and Social Media peak in 2016 and 2017 (\(p < .001\)). Generative AI peaks in 2026 (\(30.2\%\), \(p < .001\)), rising throughout without cresting within it (see Table 1, and Appendix B for the fitted trajectories).

The peak is the maximum of the fitted curve; a peak in the first or last year of the observation period indicates a cluster that declines or rises throughout rather than one that crests within it. The case of Generative AI
The boundaries between technology clusters are soft, and meaningfully display the semantic similarities between distinct technology clusters. This is also the case for Generative AI, situated in proximity to Algorithms & Recommendations; and and AR, VR & Robots. Yet, the new consumer technology clearly occupies its distinct region of the map, and has quickly become the most studied consumer technology overall (\(225\) mentions across 26 years, of which most stem from the past four years) and at the current time, making up 30.2% of all consumer technology mentions in 2026 (see also Table 1). Being a clearly ubiquitous technology, that has become the most popular subject in the academic consumer technology discourse, it is unsurprising that all leading marketing journals have devoted a substantial share of their attention to Generative AI.

title: Mapping the Field
text:
Analysis 2. Bibliometric analyses
In Analysis 2, we first analyze and map how our corpus of consumer technology literature is internally connected, and subsequently extend our bibliometric analysis to its intellectual foundation using co-citation metrics.

The field at large
On an article level, few articles discuss more than one technology cluster simultaneously, with the exception of Generative AI and AR, VR & Robots (\(12\) co-mentions), Smartphones & Apps and Computers & Software (\(12\) co-mentions); and Internet & Broadcasting and Computers & Software (\(9\) co-mentions), indicating that consumer technologies are usually discussed as a single object of study, not as a component to a larger scope. The full matrix of co-mentions across all 16 clusters is reported in the Appendix C).
Within our corpus but across articles, we find a total of \(7,115\) citation links. Within-cluster links are more prevalent than cross-cluster links in both directions, with the extent of internal coherence inversely proportional to the size of the cluster. Adopting the perspective of journals, we find similar patterns: Articles published in any specific journal cite articles from that journal more frequently than from any of the other journals. We find that IJRM and JAMS, both journals focusing on applied research, source from the other journals more frequently than vice-versa. Bi-directional links are prominent in particular between JM, MS, and JMR. Full tables summarizing the links between clusters, and between journals, can be found in the Appendix C).
Zooming out beyond the articles inside our corpus, we identify 13 labeled communities of intellectual themes discussed in the \(500\) most cited references using co-citation analysis and Louvain clustering (Aria & Cuccurullo, 2017; Blondel et al., 2008). Prior to clustering, we manually removed pure method papers, that is, references concerned solely with a method rather than its application to any topic. We manually label each community based on the shared themes of its top 10 references. Louvain clustering resulted in several small communities in which no clear theme could be identified, which we summarize under “Other” so as not to break the top 500 reference inclusion we set. Across the corpus of consumer technology research, the top 500 references were cited a total of \(4,344\) times. For each community, we calculate its proportional dominance by dividing the citations it receives by the total citations, creating a cross-corpus overall distribution of themes discussed. The themes, their distribution and the top five references for each are summarized in Table 2. The two most dominant communities center on Algorithm and AI Perception, including algorithm aversion (23.0%), and on Online Virality and Word of Mouth (22.4%). Comparing the distribution of themes within each cluster against the overall distribution using Dirichlet posteriors, we find that technology clusters do not draw on the themes equally across the board: mature (defined as the duration since its peak, see Analysis 1) and larger clusters cover a broader intellectual foundation, indicating that they have been discussed from multiple perspectives, whereas newer technologies rest on narrower, more pointed foundations.

The case of Generative AI
The Generative AI cluster departs from established patterns both within the corpus and, at a larger scale, in the co-citation analysis. Within the corpus, articles published on Generative AI act as attention magnets, receiving disproportionately many citations from other consumer technology clusters, especially from AR, VR & Robots (22.0% of its citations) and Algorithms & Recommendations (19.6%). Generative AI does not reciprocate this connection, relying primarily on articles published within its own cluster. Given the novelty of the technology this self-containedness follows, yet given its size the cluster would be expected to be more interconnected.
The co-citation analysis reveals the same concentration. Generative AI draws primarily on Algorithm and AI Perception, indicating that current studies predominantly discuss how AI is perceived. Despite making up the majority of consumer technology publications in 2026, the substance discussed remains narrow.

title: Mapping the Field
text:
Analysis 3. Media comparison
In Analysis 3, we contrast the academic attention devoted to consumer technologies with the media attention devoted to these same technologies. Our goal in this study is to identify and quantify the relationship between interests in research, and what concerns the public.

The field at large
Across \(901\) queries, we retrieve a total of \(4,714,445\) media stories from \(4,074,851\) unique media titles. Across all sixteen technology clusters, academic attention is spread differently from media attention (\(G(15) = 1033.62\), \(p < .001\), \(w = .86\)). Nine of the sixteen clusters hold a larger share in academic attention, seven in media attention. Measured in percentage points, the largest differences on the media side are Internet & Broadcasting (\(-10.6\) pp) and Social Media (\(-8.5\) pp), and on the academic side Generative AI (\(+10.1\) pp) and Algorithms & Recommendations (\(+5.3\) pp). Figure 4 reports all clusters. All gaps diverge credibly from the media distribution, which is used as the prior. The gaps are not uniform across journals, since not all journals focus on the clusters equally.
Across the sixteen clusters, the cross-correlations between the annual academic and media shares range from \(-0.52\) to \(0.90\). The lag at which the correlation is highest is positive for ten clusters, zero for one, and negative for five, falling at the boundary of the tested range for three. A lag of four years is the most frequent, being the highest-correlating lag for five clusters, indicating that media attention generally precedes academic publications by several years. The relationship is nonetheless weak for most clusters: nine of the sixteen peak below \(r = .40\), and three peak at the boundary of the tested window, so their true lag may lie outside the range examined. Table 3 reports the correlation at every lag for all clusters. We compare the duration between peak academic and media attention for all clusters. The median difference between academic and media peaks is largest for the Journal of Marketing, with a median lag of \(-5\). Both JAMS and IJRM are ahead by a median of \(1\) compared to media attention.
We report the full measures for all comparisons and robustness checks comparing overall media attention (i.e. share of technology articles compared to all articles) against overall academic attention in Appendix E.

The case of Generative AI
Generative AI is the cluster with the largest academic over-representation, holding the largest academic share of any cluster (\(14.1\%\) overall, and \(30.2\%\) at its current peak annual share in 2026, see Table 1) and the largest positive gap of any cluster (\(+10.1\) pp, \(q < .001\)). Media attention towards Generative AI has rapidly increased in recent years, but not at the pace seen in our corpus, where it became the most discussed cluster overall and more dominant still in the current publication agenda. It is also the only cluster whose annual academic and media series correlate above \(.65\) at every lag examined, from \(.657\) to \(.905\), against a maximum of \(.724\) for any other cluster, indicating that the two trajectories rise together rather than one tracking the other.

title: Mapping the Field
text:
The case of Generative AI
Across three analyses, we discuss the case of Generative AI in contrast to earlier consumer technologies. We demonstrate that Generative AI shows diverging patterns within academic literature (Analysis 1 and 2) and also compared with media attention (Analysis 3). But why?
Our analysis suggests several explanations: First, Generative AI has penetrated almost every aspect of consumers’, marketers, and researchers lives, which offers ample opportunities for research questions. Second, Generative AI is being integrated into many existing consumer technologies, rooting it in a rich theoretical foundation that can possibly be drawn from, but also offering ample opportunities to validate and deepen our understanding of existing theories relating to consumer technologies in a new light. Third, Generative AI may be among the most accessible consumer technologies of the past quarter-century to study empirically, with a very low barrier to entry (e.g. Joerling, 2026). While efforts have been made to ease the provision of realistic stimuli for other technologies (e.g., Roggenkamp et al., 2025), Generative AI is not only accessible to study but also makes more complex study designs feasible, through easier access to custom coding and interface generation (e.g., Binz et al., 2025).
de Bellis et al. (2026) argue that consumer technology research should focus on what matters to the beneficiaries of its findings. In the case of Generative AI, the field seems to fulfill this demand: Research on the topic has risen drastically since the introduction of ChatGPT 3.5 (OpenAI, 2022) and shows no sign of slowing down — as is the attention devoted to it in media stories. This concurrent response to a new consumer technology marks a first in 26 years of consumer technology research, and suggests that the massive penetration of this technology into many aspects of our daily lives and work has a multifold effect: The relevance and ubiquity makes the topic rich to study, attractive for journals to publish (despite earlier technologies being more concentrated on specific journals, Generative AI has been adopted and published across the board), and interesting to researchers. Especially as Generative AI transforms many existing consumer technologies such as Crypto & Fintech (Winder et al., 2025), or Social Media (Møller et al., 2026), it offers ample opportunities to be applied to familiar and important paradigms in consumer technology research.
This does however not (yet) happen to a substantive extent: While one might hypothesize that the ubiquity of Generative AI also leads to integrated and interconnected research, our bibliometric analyses show the opposite pattern: Compared to other technology clusters, research on Generative AI is more self-referential and self-contained rather than interconnected with neighboring technologies. the majority of themes studied in connection with Generative AI relate to Algorithm and AI Perception. While this research is undoubtedly relevant, the apparent ubiquity of the technology leads us to urge researchers to look beyond the perception of AI itself: and towards what it can do to consumer experience: fields such as relationships, or online virality and word of mouth are currently credibly below the overall baseline, yet developments in AI call for a better understanding of its impact on these aspects of consumer behavior [sources].
